target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove scheduling barriers for voters.
objection: Designating Election Day as a federal holiday does not guarantee private-sector workers paid time off or even schedule changes, because federal holiday status mainly affects public/government calendars and leaves private employers free to set their own policies.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday would help the Americans most constrained by work schedules.
objection: Low-income workers are disproportionately concentrated in hourly retail and service jobs with less flexibility and less wage cushion, so they are the least likely to benefit from holiday status and the most likely to still face work obligations or wage loss.

target: AG1’s conclusion that a national holiday would broadly reduce voting barriers for low-income workers.
objection: Even if the date is a holiday, low-income workers may still have to work or lose wages, so the practical scheduling barrier to voting remains for them; therefore the holiday does not reliably improve their access.

target: AG1’s view that the holiday would improve turnout and should therefore be adopted.
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase turnout compared with other voting-access reforms, so it is not a reliable standalone solution.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would help low-income workers because it changes schedules.
objection: Federal holiday status primarily changes schedules for public institutions, not private employers, so it does not guarantee usable, compensated time off for private-sector workers.

target: AG1’s assumption that holiday status would meaningfully reduce barriers for those who need relief most.
objection: The workers most constrained by work schedules are the ones least likely to get useful leave from a holiday alone, because low-income hourly workers still face wage-loss risk or continued work obligations.

target: AG1’s argument that a national holiday would be a reliable voting-access reform.
objection: If the reform does not reliably reduce the core barrier for the people most affected, then it is disadvantageous relative to more direct alternatives such as state time-off requirements for voting or automatic voter registration.

target: AG1’s claim that treating Election Day as a holiday would elevate democracy and encourage participation.
objection: Voting turnout depends on whether people can practically vote within their time and work constraints; if the binding constraint remains, motivational framing alone will not reliably increase actual voting for those affected.

target: AG1’s implication that a holiday would ensure employees can vote without work conflict.
objection: A federal national holiday does not legally require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so employees’ ability to vote still depends on employer discretion rather than the holiday label.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would especially help people constrained by work schedules.
objection: Low-income workers are disproportionately in hourly retail and service jobs with less scheduling flexibility, so many of them still face wage-loss or labor constraints even if Election Day is a holiday.

target: AG1’s broader conclusion that holiday framing would boost participation among those blocked by work.
objection: If low-income hourly workers still face wage or work constraints, their voting is not mainly limited by civic motivation, so the holiday’s framing effect cannot overcome the remaining practical barrier.

target: AG1’s assertion that Election Day as a holiday reduces the main voting barrier.
objection: The key voting barrier is the opportunity cost of taking time during working hours without losing wages, and a federal holiday does not create an enforceable right to paid time off or schedule changes for private-sector workers.

target: AG1’s assumption that the holiday would help the workers most constrained by schedules.
objection: Low-income workers are concentrated in hourly retail and service jobs with less flexibility and less wage cushion, so for them the opportunity-cost barrier remains even if Election Day is a federal holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday would be a fair national solution.
objection: Because relief would depend on employer discretion, the policy would produce uneven outcomes and could worsen unequal access across income groups, disadvantaging low-income workers.

target: AG1’s argument that broad support and OECD precedent favor the policy.
objection: More reliable reforms exist that directly target the constraints on voting, such as state laws requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration, so those are better policy choices than a holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday reduces real-world schedule overlap enough to help voters.
objection: A holiday may close or adjust schools and prompt some workplaces to alter hours, but it still does not require private employers to provide paid leave, so it only partially reduces scheduling barriers.

target: AG1’s implication that the holiday would help the relevant workers because it changes calendars.
objection: A federal holiday does not legally compel private employers to close or give paid time off, so hourly workers can still face lost wages or continued work obligations when voting during work hours.

target: AG1’s belief that the holiday would not hurt low-income workers.
objection: Because low-income workers are the most likely to face work or wage constraints and the holiday does not reliably remove them, adopting the holiday as the national approach would disadvantage their voting access.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would improve access for everyone in practice.
objection: Holiday status would create uneven schedule relief, with low-income hourly workers bearing the greatest work and wage costs, so it would not improve access evenly or reliably.

target: AG1’s broader conclusion that the holiday should be the national solution.
objection: Voting-access policy should prioritize the people most constrained by practical barriers, and because the holiday leaves private-employer outcomes uneven, direct reforms like time-off requirements and automatic voter registration are better choices.

target: AG2’s claim that a national holiday would disadvantage low-income workers’ voting access.
objection: A policy that does not require employers or schools to impose extra work demands or wage loss cannot inherently disadvantage low-income workers’ ability to vote; at most, it may produce uneven levels of accommodation, not a built-in worsening of access.

target: AG2’s assumption that holiday status creates new work or wage burdens.
objection: A national holiday is mainly a societal and institutional signal, not a mandate that private employers cut pay or schedule extra work, so it does not inherently create new work or wage burdens for workers.

target: AG2’s argument that the holiday should be rejected because it is ineffective and harmful.
objection: Treating Election Day as a holiday frames voting as important civic participation rather than a chore, which can elevate democracy and encourage participation.

target: AG2’s suggestion that there is no strong basis for the policy.
objection: The measure has broad domestic support and international precedent, with 71% of Democrats, 59% of Republicans, and 27 of 36 OECD countries supporting or using holiday/weekend election timing.
